opening_message:
Ticket 1: Karen Black (employee ID E008) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E008.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Karen Black (E008) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting admin access to Source Code. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, not Payroll Specialist, so admin is not permitted. Maximum allowed is write; recommend granting write (requested admin exceeds max).
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB for E008 (Karen Black) shows contractor with basic security training, contradicting the earlier note's full-time status. As a contractor, admin is never permitted; write requires advanced training (she has basic). Maximum allowed is read, and requested admin exceeds the max, so recommend granting read.
reason: E008 (Karen Black) requests admin access to Source Code, but the notes conflict: HR lists her as full-time (max write, admin not allowed since Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code), while Security lists her as a contractor with basic security training (contractors never get admin; write requires advanced training). Given the contradictory employment records and the security database's verified contractor status, the safe maximum is read. Admin exceeds the max, so grant read (the maximum allowed under the more restrictive valid interpretation).

content.text:
Let me work through this. The ticket: Karen Black (E008) requests admin access to Source Code.

The two notes from HR and Security disagree:
- Note 1: HR says role Payroll Specialist, employment type full_time, recommends write for Source Code. Max for full_time is write (admin only if role owns system; role is Payroll Specialist, system Source Code owned by Engineer, so admin not permitted). Requested admin > max write, so grant write.
- Note 2: Security says role Payroll Specialist, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommends read. Contractor: read, or write if advanced training. She has basic, so max read. Requested admin > read, grant read.

The notes conflict on employment type. Note 1 - did HR look up in own database? Note 1 says "looked up in own database before writing" for role and employment type. Note 2 says employment type "looked up in own database before writing" and security training "looked up in own database before writing", but role "not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1".

So both looked up employment type in their own databases, but they differ. Hmm. This is a contradiction. The Security agent presumably has a security database. HR has HR database.

Which to trust? The team has conflicting facts. As the Approver, I need to make a decision. Let me think about the standard policy.

The access policy depends on employment type and security training. For contractors, write is allowed with advanced security training. Security note says contractor with basic training, max read. HR note says full-time, max write.

How to resolve? Typically in these scenarios, the security DB is authoritative for security-related attributes, and HR for employment. But here they conflict on employment type. Note 1 says full_time looked up; Note 2 says contractor looked up. Both claim to have looked up in their own databases. This is contradictory information.

Given conflicting evidence, the safer approach is to grant the lower level (least privilege). The security note recommends read. Requested admin. Maximum under contractor-with-basic is read. Under full-time is write. Since we can't be certain, granting the lower of the two possible maximums (read) aligns with security best practice. Also the security agent verified contractor status and training in their own database.

Actually, let me consider. The Approver must decide based on available info. There's a conflict. The principle of least privilege suggests granting read (the maximum allowed under the more restrictive interpretation). Granting write would assume full-time, but security says contractor. Given the contradiction, grant read.

Let me submit read with reasoning.
